lede: Stand a pencil in a glass of water and it looks broken at the surface. Light changes speed when it crosses from one material into another, and changing speed makes it change direction. That one idea explains the broken pencil, the bent ray in a glass block, and the band of colours a prism throws on a wall.
can: Draw the normal at each face and measure both angles from it
Explain a bend using the words change of speed, not optical density
Describe how a prism splits white light, in the right colour order

md: A straw in a glass of juice looks snapped in half at the surface. Nothing has happened to the straw. Light travels more slowly in water than in air, and a change of speed makes it change direction — so the light reaching your eye comes from the wrong place.

md:
Where the ray meets the glass, draw the **normal**: a line at right angles to the surface. The angle between the arriving ray and the normal is the **angle of incidence**; the angle inside the glass is the **angle of refraction**.
Here 50° becomes 31°, so the ray has bent **towards** the normal. That bending is **refraction**.

prompt: In the glass-block diagram, which line are the angles of incidence and refraction both measured from?
options: the normal, drawn at right angles to the surface
the surface of the glass block
the bottom edge of the block
answer: the normal, drawn at right angles to the surface
explain: Both angles are measured from the normal. Drawing that dashed line first is the habit that makes every optics question the same question.

md:
Light travels more slowly in glass than in air. A row of people marching in step onto grass does the same thing: the end that crosses first shortens its stride first, so the whole row swings round.
That is the whole mechanism. **Slower means bent towards the normal; faster means bent away from it**, and the bigger the change of speed, the bigger the bend.

title: Why speed, and not density?
md: Calling glass "denser" names a property; it does not explain anything. The change of **speed** is what the examiner wants, because it is the thing that actually causes the turn — and it is the same sentence whether the light is entering glass, water or perspex.

prompt: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block. What causes it to change direction at the surface?
options: the light slows down as it enters the glass
the glass is more optically dense than the air
the light bounces off the surface of the glass
answer: the light slows down as it enters the glass
explain: The change of speed is the cause. Optical density is a label for the property, not an explanation, and CCEA examiners have refused it.

md:
A block has two faces, so there are two bends. Going in, the light slows and bends **towards** the normal. Coming out, it speeds up again and bends **away** from the normal, by exactly as much.
So the **emergent ray** is parallel to the incident ray. It has been moved sideways, not turned. Draw a fresh normal at the second face: the first one is no use there.

prompt: A ray enters the top face of a rectangular glass block and leaves through the bottom face. Compared with the ray that went in, the emergent ray is __ to it. (one word)
explain: Parallel. The bend on the way in and the bend on the way out are equal and opposite, so the direction is restored and only the position shifts.

md:
**Question.** The diagram marks 35° between the ray and the surface of the block. State the angle of incidence.
**Step 1** — draw the normal, at right angles to the surface. The reason: every angle in optics is measured from it.
**Step 2** — the normal and the surface are at right angles, so the two angles add to 90°.
**Step 3** — 90° − 35° = 55°.
**Answer** — the angle of incidence is 55°, and the ray bends towards the normal as it enters.

prompt: A diagram marks 28° between a ray and the flat surface of a glass block. What is the angle of incidence, in degrees?
explain: 90° − 28° = 62°. Whenever the printed angle sits against the surface, subtract it from 90° before you do anything else.

md:
A prism has two faces that are not parallel, so its two bends do not cancel: they **add**. That is why the light leaves a prism travelling in a clearly different direction, while light leaving a rectangular block does not.
Draw a normal at **both** faces. A prism diagram with no normals cannot be marked, whichever way up the prism is drawn.

title: What examiners wrote about the prism diagram
md: **Summer 2025 Higher Q8:** a prism drawn point-down confused many candidates, a significant number **left the normal out altogether**, and some bent the upper ray **towards** the normal as it left the glass instead of away from it.

prompt: Why does light leaving a triangular prism travel in a different direction from the light that entered it, while light leaving a rectangular block does not?
options: the prism's two faces are not parallel, so its two bends add together
a prism is made of a different kind of glass from a block
light is only refracted once in a prism
answer: the prism's two faces are not parallel, so its two bends add together
explain: The shape does it. In a block the two faces are parallel and the bends cancel; in a prism they are not, so the bends add.

text: 6. Dispersion: the same rule, seven times over

alt: A wide band of spectrum colours thrown by a prism onto a pale wall, running continuously from red at one edge through orange, yellow and green to blue and violet at the other.
caption: A real spectrum on a wall. One colour runs into the next; there are no separate stripes.
prompt: The colours at one edge of this band have been slowed most in the glass. Which edge is it, and what is the name for this band of colours?

md:
White light is already a mixture of colours. Each colour travels at a slightly different speed in glass, so each is refracted by a slightly different amount and they arrive separated. Splitting them this way is called **dispersion**; the band of colours is a **spectrum**.
**red** changes speed least, so it is refracted least. **violet** changes speed most, so it is refracted most.

prompt: White light passes through a glass prism and lands on a screen as a band of colours. What is the one-word name for that band of colours?
explain: Spectrum. "Rainbow" is the word examiners see most often and cannot credit — a rainbow is something that happens in the sky; a spectrum is what a prism produces.

md:
Draw round the block, send a ray in from the ray box and mark the ray going in and the ray coming out with pencil crosses. Lift the block, join the marks, draw the normal, and measure both angles with a protractor.
Repeat for a spread of angles of incidence — a sensible range in steps of about 10°, not three readings bunched together.

title: Refraction: the CCEA Prescribed Practical
why: The only video we have made for this board's own practical: the ray box, the pencil marks and the protractor, done properly.

prompt: In Prescribed Practical P5, why is the glass block drawn round on the paper before the ray is traced?
options: so the block can be lifted and the marks joined to show the ray inside it
so the block can be weighed afterwards
so the ray box does not move during the experiment
answer: so the block can be lifted and the marks joined to show the ray inside it
explain: You never see the ray inside the glass on the paper. Outlining the block lets you lift it, join the entry and exit marks, and measure the angles from the normal.

md:
Plot angle of incidence across and angle of refraction up, then draw one **smooth curve** through the points — never a ruler from dot to dot.
As the angle of incidence increases the angle of refraction increases too, but not in step with it: the graph is a curve, and it is not a straight line through the origin. The wording the scheme wants is **related but not proportional**.

prompt: On the P5 graph of angle of refraction against angle of incidence, the points lie on a smooth curve through the origin. What does that tell you about the two angles?
options: they are related but not proportional
they are not related to each other at all
answer: they are related but not proportional
explain: Related but not proportional. "Directly proportional" is only for a straight line through the origin, and the reason to give is that this graph is a curve.

title: PhET: Bending Light
attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder, licensed under CC BY-NC 4.0 (https://phet.colorado.edu)
task: Set the lower material to glass and turn on the protractor. Take five pairs of angles as you swing the source round, and check for yourself that doubling the angle of incidence does not double the angle of refraction. Then open the Prisms screen, switch the source to white light and find which colour bends most.

prompt: In the Bending Light simulation you set the lower material to glass and double the angle of incidence. What happens to the angle of refraction?
options: it increases, but by less than double
answer: it increases, but by less than double
explain: It increases, but by less than double. That is exactly what the curve on the P5 graph is telling you, and it is why the two angles are related but not proportional.

md:
Draw the normal at every face and measure both angles from it.
Explain a bend as a change of speed: slower bends towards the normal, faster away from it.
Turn an angle printed to the surface into an angle of incidence by subtracting from 90°.
Describe dispersion by a prism, name the spectrum and put the colours in order.
Carry out P5, plot the graph and say that the two angles are related but not proportional.

This comes as a printed diagram with a mark for each feature. The first mark is almost always the **normal**, drawn as a dashed line at right angles to the surface; the last is usually the direction of the bend, or the word on the answer line. If you are stuck on a bend, ask which way the speed changed: slower is towards the normal, faster is away from it. Never write "rainbow" where the answer is spectrum.
